newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Channel rail link - trainspotter buyers' next play?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Channel rail link - trainspotter buyers' next play?.

text.p: Britain's private sector transport boom has spawned a new breed of rail enthusiast to stand beside traditional anorak-wearing fans -- the investor trainspotter.

Interest took off when the break-up of the nationalised network British Rail began in 1995. The cut-price sell-off of Railtrack Plc in 1996 and 25 passenger rail franchises to private sector players has revitalised investment in British transport.
With investors' appetites now whetted, the next big action could be the Channel Tunnel rail link between Britain and France.

The three billion pound ($4.9 billion) venture -- one of the biggest civil engineering projects since World War Two -- will be floated in 1998 as part of its parent group on the London Stock Exchange, with a possible dual listing in New York.
The flotation is expected to raise more than one billion pounds in equity.

Behind the project is London and Continental Railways (LCR), a consortium embracing financiers and transport groups which also owns the Channel Tunnel passenger train Eurostar which links London with Paris and Brussels.
LCR says it is still considering whether to follow Railtrack's lead by employing a dual listing.

"We've not yet decided," LCR director Jeremy Canfield told Reuters. "But we're conscious of what Railtrack did and some of the same people are involved. Once we have a clear idea of the flotation plans we will set up investor roadshows."
In addition to the equity issue, LCR plans to raise "several billion" in debt.
BOOST FOR BUILDERS
The rail link also comes as a welcome boost to the British construction industry at a time when public infrastructure spending is being cut.
LCR expects well over a billion pounds' worth of contracts to be put up for tender in the coming months.

The consortium -- comprising National Express Group Plc, the Virgin Group, SBC Warburg, London Electricity Plc and engineering group Bechtel -- won the government contract to build the fast link from London to the Channel Tunnel at Folkestone last February.
Part of the deal was ownership of the Eurostar passenger rail company.
LCR plans a stock market flotation and major debt issue to raise the cash for building the link. The consortium itself doesn't get paid until the job is almost done.

"The cost of construction is three billion at 1995 prices plus the financial charges involved. But the government subsidy of just under three billion does not start to feed through until two-thirds of the construction costs have already been spent," Canfield said.
FUNDING RACE UNDERWAY
A race against the clock is underway to set up financing to build the link by its deadline of 2003. Late delivery will mean penalties.
LCR fought off intense competition to build a 108 kilometre (66-mile) fast rail link between London and the coastal connection to the Channel Tunnel.
LCR aims eventually to feed through trains from the rest of Britain and Europe onto its fast-link, connecting cities across Europe.

The aim is to cut rail journey times to the continent through the tunnel. Eurostar was thrown in free as part of the package and will be a key asset in the group once LCR goes to the market for capital.
EUROSTAR KEY IN FINANCIAL JIGSAW
Therefore, Eurostar's performance is crucial to the building of the rail link itself.

Eurostar has witnessed a marketing-led rejuvenation since being taken over by LCR. More aggressive promotion of its exisiting services have been supplemented with plans for a new ski service to the French Alps.

Bumping up passenger numbers is crucial for a timely and successful floatation. By the end of 1996, passenger numbers were around six million, almost double 1995 levels. Eurostar has said it needs 10 million passengers a year to break even.
"For the flotation to go ahead three things have to be right," said Canfield. "First Eurostar has to improve its financial performance.
"Second, we have to further develop the design of the high-speed link. It has to be at a more advanced stage so that at least the bulk of the sub contracts are in place.
"Third, is the state of the financial markets."
REPEAT OF EUROTUNNEL WOES?
LCR is wary of one particular criticism -- that it could repeat the mistakes of the company behind the construction project of the decade, Channel Tunnel's debt-laden parent Eurotunnel Plc.
But Canfield played down the possibilties that LCR will suffer from the same problems which led to Eurotunnel delivering its project late and at huge expense.

"First, a number of things are different this time -- our design is at a more advanced stage even before we let the contracts. Second, we have our safety case already in place. Third, one of Eurotunnel's biggest cost over-runs was the rolling stock. It was also a logistically constrained underground working environment," Canfield said.
"Our contracts are incentivised (in line with industry practice) so there is risk sharing between sub-contractors and ourselves in both directions."
These incentives include bonuses for finishing early and penalties for delays, he said.
As Eurotunnel itself continues to grapple with its nine billion pounds of debt, Canfield insists "the rail link will not be another Eurotunnel." ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
